mcqs.question: Why is merge sort the natural fit for sorting a linked list rather than quicksort?
options: Quicksort only works on data types that support hashing
Merge sort has a better worst-case time complexity than quicksort in every situation
Merge sort's split and merge steps rely only on sequential pointer-following, while quicksort's partition step depends on the O(1) random access an array provides
Linked lists cannot be sorted with quicksort at all
mcqs.explanation: Splitting a list at its midpoint and merging two sorted sequences both work purely by following `next` pointers, which a list supports natively; quicksort's partitioning leans on comparing and swapping elements at arbitrary positions, which costs a linear scan per comparison on a list. Quicksort can technically be adapted to lists, just awkwardly, and merge sort's worst case matches quicksort's average, not universally beats it.

mcqs.question: In the list merge-sort split step, why is a `prev` pointer maintained one step behind the `slow` pointer?
options: So the recursion can be converted into an iterative loop
To sever the list into two halves at the midpoint, since `slow` alone locates the midpoint but leaves no way to cut the link there
To detect whether the list has a cycle before sorting
To reverse the first half of the list in place
mcqs.explanation: Fast/slow pointers alone can identify the midpoint node but can't disconnect the list — you need the node just before the midpoint to set its `next` to None. `prev` exists purely to make that cut, not for cycle detection, reversal, or converting recursion to iteration.

mcqs.question: Compared to array merge sort, why does linked-list merge sort typically use less auxiliary space?
options: Merging re-links existing nodes in place instead of writing into a freshly allocated output array, leaving only O(log n) recursion-stack space
Linked lists don't need to be split before merging
The list version doesn't use recursion
List nodes are smaller in memory than array elements
mcqs.explanation: Array merge sort's merge step needs a separate output buffer to hold sorted results, costing O(n) space; the list version merges by re-pointing existing nodes, so the only extra space is the O(log n) recursion depth. Both versions split before merging, both typically use recursion, and node size isn't the reason for the space difference.

mcqs.question: Why does adapting quicksort's partition step to a linked list give up quicksort's main real-world advantage?
options: Because linked lists cannot store numeric values
Because array quicksort's speed comes from O(1) in-place swaps with good cache behavior, and a list has no equivalent — sublists must be built by re-linking one node at a time instead
Because quicksort requires the input to already be partially sorted
Because a linked list's pivot element cannot be compared to other elements
mcqs.explanation: Array quicksort's practical edge is fast, cache-friendly in-place swapping via index arithmetic — a list has no positions to swap, so the adapted version ends up building new sublists by relinking nodes, which is effectively a differently-shaped merge without quicksort's benefit. Nothing prevents value comparison or numeric storage on a list, and quicksort doesn't require pre-sorted input.

mcqs.question: Merging k sorted lists one at a time into a growing result list costs O(nk). Merging them in tournament-bracket rounds instead costs O(n log k). Why is the rounds approach faster?
options: It uses a hash map to avoid comparisons entirely
It sorts each list individually first, which the one-at-a-time approach skips
Each round only ever merges two lists together at a time, and halving the list count each round takes log k rounds instead of k sequential merges against a growing result
It requires converting the lists to arrays first, which is inherently faster
mcqs.explanation: The one-at-a-time approach re-scans the ever-growing merged result against each new list, k times over; pairing lists up per round means every merge is a simple two-list merge, and halving the list count each round takes only log k rounds total. No hash map or array conversion is involved, and both approaches assume the input lists are already individually sorted.

mcqs.question: Reordering a list as L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1, … looks like it needs random access to elements from the back. How is it solved on a singly linked list without that access?
options: By converting the list to an array, reordering it there, then rebuilding the list
By combining three existing list techniques in sequence: find the middle, reverse the second half, then merge the two halves by alternating nodes
It cannot be done without a doubly linked list
By repeatedly finding the last node with a full traversal for every output position
mcqs.explanation: The list-native solution composes primitives already available on a singly linked list — fast/slow midpoint-finding, in-place reversal, and alternating merge — rather than needing true random access or an array conversion. It doesn't require a doubly linked list, and repeatedly re-traversing to find the last node for every position would be far worse than O(n) overall.
